newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland's "G7" business group calls for calm.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland's "G7" business group calls for calm.

text.p: Northern Ireland business leaders, worried by growing tension over a Protestant parade, called on divided Protestants and Catholics not to do anything which might wreck the province's economic prospects.
"Neither community will gain if we blow our economic prospects," the group, which calls itself G7 said in a statement.

"Regions all over Europe are in cut-throat competition for jobs and investment. People in Northern Ireland are entitled to their fair share, and more indeed, since paramilitary violence has denied them that share for the past 25 years." it said.
G7, which includes the Confederation of British Industry, hoteliers, the Institute of Directors, Chamber of Commerce and Trades Unions, said agreement should be reached on divisive issues.
The statement was issued ahead of a decision whether to ban, permit or reroute an Orange Order parade at Drumcree, near Portadown, on Sunday.

The Orange Order says the march, which it plans to end by parading down the Catholic Garvaghy Road area of Portadown, is a birthright but Irish nationalists say it is sectarian intimidation and should be banned.

The same march last year sparked the worst violence in decades and caused millions of pounds (dollars) of damage and an incalculable blemish on Northern Ireland's reputation as a place for foreign investment and job creation, business leaders say.
G7 said the population was entitled to expect jobs and prosperity after an investment drive by business leaders and the government's IDB investment arm.

"They will only get it if all of us, however much we disagree on other matters, unite on one thing, namely a determination not to let our disagreement wreck the economic prospects which it is in everybody's interests to protect and enhance," the group said.
The group voiced disquiet about the consequences of violence over coming weeks, the climax of the Protestant "marching season" which inflames passions every year.

"Even if - hopefully - trouble is averted this summer, the dark shadow in which we have all lived in recent months must surely strengthen everyone's determination to renew their commitment and intensify their efforts to remove that shadow for once and for all," the statement said.

"No society can teeter indefinitely on the brink. We need to devise a framework within which disputes over conflicting rights can be resolved in a way which does not risk inflicting harm on the wider community or sabotaging its vital economic interests and therefore ruining the prospects for jobs and investment."
Last year was a record for foreign investment in Northern Ireland, which touts itself as an ideal location for electronic, hi-tech and software projects from the United States and Asia.
According to official figures, investment totalled 490 million pounds sterling against 432 million in 1995/96 and 252 million in 1994/95.
